name: Face yoga / face exercises

card.summary: Repeated facial-muscle movements promoted for toning and de-puffing the face; small studies exist but good evidence for appearance changes is limited.
card.aka: Facial exercises, facial yoga, facial gymnastics
card.note: Available trials are small, and studies on puffiness are mostly in surgical or TMD patients rather than healthy people.

quick.overview:
Face yoga refers to routines of facial muscle contractions, stretches and massage-like movements. It is marketed for anti-aging and, in looksmaxxing circles, for reducing puffiness and improving facial tone.

Published research is sparse. There is a 2014 systematic review of facial exercises for rejuvenation, a small 2025 pre-experimental study in 12 middle-aged women, and trials in other settings such as temporomandibular dysfunction and swelling after nose surgery.
quick.mechanism: Proponents propose that exercising facial muscles increases their tone and bulk and may help move fluid. Researchers have measured outcomes such as muscle tonus, stiffness and elasticity, but the proposed mechanisms for cosmetic changes remain under study.
quick.risks: Gentle facial exercise is not associated with major documented harms in the studies listed. Some people discussing the practice raise concern that repeated muscle contraction might deepen expression lines; no study cited here tested that.

lead: Face yoga, also called face exercises, is a set of routines involving repeated contraction, stretching or massage of facial muscles. It is promoted as a non-surgical way to look younger, tone the face and reduce puffiness.[1][2]

Published research is limited and small. A 2014 systematic review in Aesthetic Surgery Journal evaluated the literature on facial exercises for rejuvenation, framing the effectiveness of such approaches as still debated.[1] A 2025 pre-experimental trial in Medicina studied 12 women with a mean age near 50 over eight weeks of intensive face yoga, measuring facial muscle tonus, stiffness and elasticity.[2]
In looksmaxxing communities the practice is mentioned alongside lymphatic massage and gua sha as a way to reduce facial puffiness.
infobox: Small trials and a systematic review[1][2]

paras: Face yoga programs consist of named facial movements, often performed for a set number of repetitions over several weeks. Programs are distributed via books, apps and social media. Descriptions of specific routines in the studies below vary by trial.

A 2014 systematic review in Aesthetic Surgery Journal assessed the evidence for facial exercises as facial rejuvenation, noting that nonmedical approaches such as facial exercises, acupuncture and acupressure have become more popular while their effectiveness remains debated.[1]

A 2025 pre-experimental clinical trial in Medicina enrolled 12 women (mean age about 50) and applied eight weeks of intensive face yoga, assessing facial muscle tonus, stiffness and elasticity.[2] Its small size and lack of a control group limit conclusions.

A 2024 randomized controlled trial of 90 patients with temporomandibular dysfunction compared dry needling and face yoga for pain, depression, function and sleep quality; this concerns a medical condition rather than appearance.[3]
A 2026 study in the American Journal of Otolaryngology examined face yoga for swelling and bruising after septorhinoplasty, a surgical context rather than everyday facial puffiness.[4]
